sources.title: Sudan: Driver killed in aerial attack on aid trucks in South Kordofan
sources.excerpt: The World Food Programme (WFP) has strongly condemned a deadly airstrike on two clearly marked aid trucks in South Kordofan, Sudan, this past weekend.
sources.text: Sudan: Driver killed in aerial attack on aid trucks in South Kordofan. The World Food Programme (WFP) has strongly condemned a deadly airstrike on two clearly marked aid trucks in South Kordofan, Sudan, this past weekend. A driver was killed in the attack, which occurred early on Saturday. The contracted trucks were carrying WFP food commodities and were travelling between the cities of Dilling and Kadugli. They were clearly marked as humanitarian vehicles, the UN agency said in a statement. Additional details regarding the circumstances of the incident, and the extent of the damage to the food cargo, are still being determined. WFP called for a prompt and impartial investigation into the incident and for those responsible to be held to account. The attack came just one day after a WFP truck hit an explosive device in Dilling after delivering food assistance. “These incidents underscore the increasingly challenging security environment in Sudan and the risks that aid workers face when delivering life-saving assistance to communities in need,” the statement said. WFP underlined its committed to safely delivering life-saving assistance to millions across Sudan who depend on humanitarian support. The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and former allies the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have been fighting since April 2023. Last year, more than 30 million people needed humanitarian assistance, according to the UN aid coordination office OCHA . WFP urged all those involved in the fighting to respect their obligations under international humanitarian law, protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, and ensure safe and unimpeded access for both humanitarian personnel and cargo.

sources.text: Sudan’s Al-Burhan Vows To Retake All Territory From RSF. General al-Burhan vowed to recapture all RSF-controlled territory.He rejected peace negotiations as violence against civilians continued.The conflict has displaced fourteen million people since 2023.Sudan’s military chief, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, has vowed to take “every inch” of territory that is currently under the control of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), while rejecting negotiations to end the war in the country.Al-Burhan was addressing a gathering in Village 5 in Merowe, in northern Sudan, according to the Sudan News Agency. Al-Burhan vowed to keep fighting as violence in Sudan’s West Kordofan state left 10 civilians dead and several more injured, a local charity group said according to Al Jazeera. The RSF carried out the attack, the group said.The Dar Hamar Emergency Committee said in a statement that the RSF committed multiple violations against civilians in the Abu Ajal village in the southeastern countryside of En Nahud.Massad Boulos, the US senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, in a post on X on Monday, said that peace could be achieved “through an inclusive Sudanese-owned and Sudanese-led national dialogue, transition toward a civilian-led government”. The remark sets out Washington’s latest public position on how the conflict should end.Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia And Sudan Call For Talks As Ethiopia War EscalatesWhy There’s Civil War in SudanThe civil war in Sudan started in April 2023 after months of tensions between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the RSF group. The war has reached 13 of Sudan’s 18 states and is the reason behind the displacement of 14 million people, creating one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises and killing tens of thousands of people. RSF is said to be backed by the United Arab Emirates. The roots of the current crisis trace back to 2019, when widespread public protests led to the overthrow of long-serving dictator Omar al-Bashir.After his removal, military leaders and civilian groups established a joint government to guide Sudan toward democratic elections. However, that fragile alliance was broken in October 2021, when the armed forces staged a second coup to seize sole control of the state.Drone Attacks, Siege Leave Half A Million At Risk In Sudan's El ObeidThat coup was orchestrated by two former allies who now lead opposing sides in the war: General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, head of the regular armed forces, and his then-deputy, General Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, widely known as "Hemedti," who commands the powerful paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The partnership collapsed when negotiations over transitioning back to civilian rule reached a deadlock. The central point of contention was a proposal to integrate Hemedti’s 100,000-strong RSF paramilitary into the regular national army, along with intense disagreement over who would command the unified force.With both generals unwilling to relinquish their political influence, wealth, and military dominance, political dialogue quickly dissolved into mutual suspicion.

sources.text: Global risk map reveals countries deemed 'extremely' dangerous including Iran, Yemen and Sudan with Switzerland and Norway among the safest. A new map has revealed the most dangerous places in the world. American security firm Global Guardian has published its 2027 Global Risk Map, which assesses the safety of countries around the world. The firm looks at changes in seven criteria: crime , armed conflict, terrorism, political unrest, healthcare system, infrastructure and natural disasters. Using these, it then ranks nations based on their level of risk, from low to extreme. Many of the most dangerous countries in the world lie in the Middle East and North Africa, including Iran , Yemen and Sudan. The whole of Ukraine , as well as the land in Russia bordering the nation, is also at an extreme risk. Conversely, almost all of the lowest risk countries are dotted around Europe, and include Switzerland, Norway and Denmark. The UK has been classed as a nation of moderate risk, though the Republic of Ireland was classed as a low-risk nation. The US, meanwhile, has also been designated a moderate-risk nation, however the Mexican side of the border was classed as a region of extreme risk. Many of the West's allies in the Gulf, including Jordan, Saudi Arabia , the UAE and Oman, are all classed as medium-risk countries. Global Guardian's risk map. Countries in red are classified as of being in extreme risk, those in deep orange are of a high risk, bright orange indicates a medium risk, yellow shows moderate and green shows low risk Global Guardian classified the north of Egypt's Sinai Peninsula as an area of extreme risk. The land bridge that connects North Africa and the Middle East is a key trade corridor, as well as a strategically important security buffer region. Earlier this week, Israeli finance minister Bezalel Smotrich inflamed relations with Egypt by threatening to take the peninsula if it dared to attack his nation. The comments were made ahead of the anniversary of the start of the Yom Kippur war of 1973, the month-long conflict between Israel and an Egyptian-led coalition of Gulf and North African countries, as well as North Korea. The conflict resulted in tens of thousands dead between both sides. Mr Smotrich was responding to comments made by Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi earlier on Monday, who said his nation's armed forces remained prepared to defend Egypt 'at all times and under any circumstance'. Much of north and central Africa, including Sudan, are also considered extreme-risk areas. Global Guardian said Nigeria was suffering from 'banditry, jihadism, organised crime, and intercommunal violence'. Earlier this week, armed gangs stormed an illegal mining site and a village in Nigeria's Zamfara state, killing 17 people. Bandits have for years terrorised rural communities in north-west and central Nigeria, raiding villages, abducting residents and looting and burning homes. Dozens of gang members on motorcycles swept into the mine outside Bindin village in Zamfara's Maru district on Monday, shooting dead five miners. They then entered the village and killed 12 soldiers in a shootout, authorities said. The security firm also cited Ethiopia as a nation of extreme risk, writing that the country has 'perennial conflicts with both external neighbours as well as with powerful ethnonationalist regional governments that operate their own armed forces and government structures'. Violence in the nation has resurged in recent weeks, following a devastating civil war between 2020 and 2022. In recent days Eritrean troops have been deployed around a town in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, after around two weeks of internal conflict threatening a wider regional war. Fighting broke out between the rebel Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and Ethiopian federal forces on September 23. Over the weekend, the Ethiopian army and an allied Tigrayan militia entered the regional capital of Mekelle without a fight after the TPLF pulled out. A commander with the militia told AFP his troops had reached Wukro town, roughly 30 miles north of the city, and on the main road leading to Eritrea in the north. Sources said Eritrean troops were in Adigrat, around 25 miles by road south of the Eritrean border, with some headed south towards Mekelle. Down in South America, pockets of several nations were classed as regions of extreme risk, including the whole of Venezuela, as well as land in Colombia and Brazil that borders the country. The UK's foreign office says of Venezuela: 'There is a high threat of terrorist attack globally affecting UK interests and British nationals.' It adds: 'Armed robbery, mugging, carjacking and burglary are common in parts of Venezuela and can be accompanied by extreme violence.' In June, the country faced devastating earthquakes that resulted in the La Guaira being declared a 'disaster zone'. And in January, the US launched a blitz attack that resulted in the capture of dictator Nicolás Maduro.

sources.title: Sudan’s al-Burhan rejects talks, vows to retake all territory from RSF
sources.excerpt: At least 10 civilians were killed in West Kordofan and 5,500 displaced in Blue Nile as clashes widened on Tuesday.
sources.text: Sudan’s al-Burhan rejects talks, vows to retake all territory from RSF. Sudan’s military chief, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, has promised to seize “every inch” of territory under the control of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), rejecting negotiations to end three and a half years of war. Al-Burhan made the comments on Tuesday while addressing a gathering in Village 5, located in the northern Sudanese locality of Merowe, according to the Sudan News Agency. He said the “military option” would continue until the RSF was removed from Sudan. The Sudanese army and the RSF have been fighting since April 2023 after leaders of the groups fell out over plans to integrate the paramilitary force into Sudan’s army. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million , according to UN and international estimates. Al-Burhan’s pledge to continue fighting came as 10 civilians were killed and several others were wounded in an attack by the RSF in Sudan’s West Kordofan state, according to a local charity group. In a statement, the Dar Hamar Emergency Committee accused the RSF of multiple violations against civilians in Abu Ajal village in the southeastern countryside of En Nahud. The RSF has been massing in West Kordofan as Sudan’s army advances towards the cities of En Nahud and Al Khuway after gains in neighbouring North Kordofan. In Sudan’s Blue Nile state, more than 5,500 people were displaced from villages over three days amid deteriorating security, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Tuesday. Meanwhile, an envoy of US President Donald Trump said Sudanese parties must take the lead in talks to end the war. In a post on X on Monday, Massad Boulos, the US senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, said peace could be achieved “through an inclusive Sudanese-owned and Sudanese-led national dialogue, transition toward a civilian-led government”. The US State Department said last month that neither the Sudanese Armed Forces, the RSF, nor their respective leaders “represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan”.

sources.title: Sudan Gold Exports Top US$2.29 Billion in 9 Months
sources.excerpt: Sudan gold exports earned US$2.29 billion from January to September, the state mining company says, while US sanctions target gold linked to the war.
sources.text: Sudan Gold Exports Top US$2.29 Billion in 9 Months. Sudan gold exports through official channels earned US$2.292 billion from January to September 2026, the state mining company said on Tuesday 6 October. That is already more than the US$1.536 billion the central bank recorded for all of 2025. For Americans, Sudan gold exports are a sanctions story, because the US Treasury says gold has financed one side of the war. The figures, reported in Arabic by the Sudanese news site Sudan Tribune, show how much gold the army-aligned government now moves through official channels. The Sudanese Mineral Resources Company is the government body that supervises and regulates mining in Sudan, under the Ministry of Minerals. It licenses investors, oversees small-scale and industrial mines, and enforces safety and environmental rules. Its executive office met on Tuesday at the company’s headquarters in Khartoum to review results up to the end of September. A press release obtained by Sudan Tribune said the company set records in production, revenue and export earnings. Gold production reached 105% of the target the company had planned for 2026, and revenue collection reached 131% of its goal. Sudan gold exports earned US$2.292 billion over the nine months. Director general Mohamed Taher Omer thanked staff and mining partners and told them to redouble their efforts and clear obstacles facing the sector. He also stressed environmental protection, mine safety and the company’s shift to digital systems. The nine-month result builds on a strong first half. In July, the company said it had hit 111% of its production and revenue targets for January to June, Sudan Tribune reported . The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) are the national army, led by General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan. The government that runs the Ministry of Minerals and the state mining company is aligned with the army. The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) are a paramilitary group led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, widely known as Hemedti. In January 2025, the US government determined that the RSF had committed genocide in Sudan’s western Darfur region. The two forces have fought each other since April 2023, in a civil war the US Treasury links to a worsening humanitarian crisis. A fuller guide to the conflict is in our explainer on who is fighting in Sudan . Official figures cover only part of Sudan’s gold. The state mining company put national production at about 70 tonnes in 2025, while the central bank recorded official exports of only about 14 tonnes. A central bank statistical brief put the 2025 total at 14.7 tonnes, worth US$1.536 billion, according to Sudan Tribune . Finance Minister Gibril Ibrahim has said official exports did not exceed 20 tonnes in 2025. He also leads the Justice and Equality Movement, a Darfur armed group fighting the RSF, and the US Treasury sanctioned him in September 2025. Technical estimates cited by Sudan Tribune suggest that between 48% and 60% of Sudan’s gold is smuggled through informal channels. Sudan gold exports go mainly to the United Arab Emirates, and also to Oman, Qatar, Turkey, Egypt and several African countries. The government says more gold now moves through official channels. In August, Minerals Minister Nour al-Daem Taha said first-half official exports already equalled the official total for all of 2025. Washington has long linked Sudanese gold to the war. In June 2023, the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control, which runs US sanctions, blacklisted Al Junaid, an RSF-linked holding company with gold mining interests. The RSF seized the Jebel Amer gold mine in 2017, the Treasury said . Since then, gold mining and export have become a vital source of revenue for the RSF and Hemedti’s Dagalo family. On 7 January 2025, the Treasury sanctioned Hemedti himself and companies linked to the RSF, several of them in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). One target, the UAE-based Al Zumoroud and Al Yaqoot Gold & Jewellers, bought Sudanese gold, presumably for the RSF, and moved it to Dubai. Nine days later, the Treasury also sanctioned General al-Burhan , the army chief. Assets of sanctioned people and firms in the United States are blocked, and Americans are generally barred from dealing with them. For US refiners, jewellers, banks and investors exposed to the Gulf gold trade, higher Sudan gold exports through official channels do not remove that risk. In June 2026, the Treasury sanctioned new networks and urged both sides to accept a three-month humanitarian truce. The statement did not give the tonnage of Sudan gold exports, the buyers or the share sold to the United Arab Emirates. It also did not say whether the targets were set for the full year or only for the nine months. The company did not say how much of the gain came from higher volumes and how much from world gold prices. Its revenue figure was given only in Sudanese pounds, without a dollar value. The statement does not mention gold mined in areas held by the RSF, and the figures come from the company’s own count. sources.title: Sudan Still At War
sources.excerpt: William McCormick examines Sudan’s civil war, humanitarian crisis and Pope Leo XIV’s call for ceasefire, humanitarian corridors and lasting peace.
sources.text: Sudan Still At War. When Pope Leo XIV said that Sudan “has been transformed into a vast battlefield,” he underlined the dire urgency of the country’s situation. [1] Civil war has raged in Sudan since 2023, producing a desperate humanitarian crisis in a country that has known little peace in recent decades. The present conflict is rooted in a long history of contested political authority, regional inequality, and competing visions of the Sudanese state. While this history does not diminish the responsibility of today’s leaders for the violence, it does help to explain why violence has been so endemic to recent Sudanese history, and why the war has proven so resistant to resolution. sources.text: Sudan. Sudan, officially the Republic of the Sudan, is a country in Northeast Africa. It borders the Central African Republic to the southwest, Chad to the west, Libya to the northwest, Egypt to the north, the Red Sea to the east, Eritrea and Ethiopia to the southeast, and South Sudan to the south. Sudan has a population of 51.8 million people as of 2025 and occupies 1,886,068 square kilometres, making it Africa's third-largest country by area. Sudan's capital and most populous city is Khartoum.
